# Selection — TRD §15 row 17: which web-security baseline profile and version

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-20
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 17 · **Scope of:** review 3b (protocol), and TRD §13.11 **level 2** independently
**Constrained by:** TRD §10.9, §13.11, §6.1, §7.1 · PRD §7.12 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.1
**Profile:** [`test/vectors/web-security-baseline.json`](../../test/vectors/web-security-baseline.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-baseline-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-baseline-vectors.mjs) against a pinned index of the
standard
**Companions:** [row 12](./row-12-account-credential.md) is why most of ASVS's authentication chapter does not apply
as written; [row 1](./row-1-algorithm-suite.md) and the other fourteen are why its cryptography chapter is a floor
below what is already selected.

---

## The selection

```
Standard   OWASP Application Security Verification Standard 5.0.0
           Released 2025-05-30; current stable on 2026-08-20, with no stable
           successor and 5.0.1 named as the next (patch) target.
           345 requirements, 17 chapters, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Level      L2 — cumulative L1 + L2 — AS A FLOOR, not as the profile.

Profile    the floor
           + 8 named L3 requirements pulled up
           + 5 addendum controls the standard does not carry at any level
           + 1 recorded deviation

           218 requirements in scope: 210 at the floor, 8 pulled up.
            55 excluded, all with reasons; 2 of the 3 exclusions conditional
               with a trigger.

Applicability rule

  A chapter is in scope unless excluded. An exclusion carries a reason.
  A conditional exclusion carries a trigger, the way §15's deferred rows do.

  The assurance value of a baseline is in the exclusions being recorded,
  not in the inclusions passing.

Pinned, not fetched

  The profile is checked against an index of requirement identifiers and
  levels — never the requirement text — pinned by SHA-256 with its source
  URL and retrieval date. `pnpm check` never reaches the network;
  `pnpm asvs:pin` compares against the published file deliberately.
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. There is one candidate, and finding that out was the cheap part

§13.11 level 2 asks for "a recorded profile and repeatable verification of every applicable requirement". The
field of things that could supply it is small, and most of it fails on shape rather than on quality.

| Candidate              | Why not                                                                                            |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **OWASP ASVS**         | **Selected.** Requirement-level, versioned, levelled, published machine-readable                   |
| OWASP Top 10           | An awareness document. ASVS itself says it is not a standard, and it has no requirements to verify |
| NIST SSDF (SP 800-218) | Process rather than product. It says how to build securely, not what the artifact must do          |
| CIS Benchmarks         | Infrastructure and platform configuration; there is no benchmark for this shape of application     |
| SOC 2 / ISO 27001      | Organizational control regimes. An audit of a company, not a verification of a web client          |
| OWASP MASVS            | Mobile applications. The PWA is a web origin (§10.9), which is the whole point                     |

So the row's first sentence is that it is not really a choice, and **all of the actual work is in the three
things a version and a level do not say**: which requirements apply, what happens where the product cannot
satisfy one, and what the standard does not cover at all.

**Verified rather than remembered, and dated because §10.11's rule says to.** ASVS **5.0.0**, released
**2025-05-30**, is the current stable release on **2026-08-20**; the repository's only newer artifact is a
"bleeding edge" build of master marked for preview, and the next planned release is the patch 5.0.1. The
published CSV carries 345 requirements over 17 chapters at L1 = 70, L2 = 183, L3 = 92.

---

## 2. A level is a floor, and choosing one is not the selection

The obvious reading of this row is _pick L1, L2 or L3_. Taken that way it has an obvious answer — ASVS's own
guidance puts most applications at L2 — and the obvious answer is right and almost empty.

**It is empty because the controls §10.9 actually names are scattered across all three levels.** §10.9 lists
them: no unreviewed third-party script in the key-holding origin; CSP and Trusted Types where supported;
dependency integrity; service-worker update integrity; cookie attributes; origin checks on the transport
upgrade. In ASVS 5.0.0 those land at L1 (HSTS, CORS), L2 (CSP, `nosniff`, referrer policy, SBOM) and **L3**
(external asset integrity, CSP reporting, COOP, dependency provenance).

So the profile is **L2 as a floor plus eight named L3 requirements**, and the eight are named because §10.9's
threat model puts them above the level the standard assigns them:

| Pulled up | Why it is above its level here                                                                                                                            |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| V3.2.3    | DOM clobbering. L3 for an ordinary application; here the thing clobbered code reaches is a key handle                                                     |
| V3.4.7    | A CSP violation-reporting location. Without it the policy is enforced and unobserved                                                                      |
| V3.4.8    | Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy. A key-holding origin should not share a browsing-context group                                                                |
| V3.6.1    | External assets only with SRI — **pulled up in order to be superseded**, since A1 forbids them outright                                                   |
| V15.1.4   | Documenting risky components. Most applications may treat a dependency as a supply-chain abstraction; one inside the end-to-end boundary is a party to it |
| V15.1.5   | The same for dangerous functionality, and §10.10 already names the one instance                                                                           |
| V15.2.4   | Transitive dependencies from the expected repository — §10.9's "dependency integrity" in the standard's own words                                         |
| V15.2.5   | Protections around what the two documentation requirements identify, because documenting a risk and doing nothing is how documenting it fails             |

**Going to L3 wholesale was considered and is worse than it looks.** It adds 92 requirements, and their weight
is in chapters this product structurally does not have — six of V8 Authorization's thirteen, seven of V10
OAuth's thirty-six. It would produce a profile with a higher number and more unrecorded inapplicabilities,
which is the direction that makes a baseline decorative.

---

## 3. The exclusions are the profile, and one of them is a tenth of the standard

**55 of 345 requirements are excluded**, in three chapters, and every one carries a reason because an
unrecorded exclusion is how a baseline stops meaning anything.

- **V10 OAuth and OIDC — 36 requirements, not applicable.** There is no OAuth and no OIDC anywhere in the
  design: the account service authenticates its own credential (§13.9, row 12) and issues its own admission
  tokens (§13.2). **That is over a tenth of the standard dropped on one sentence**, which is precisely why the
  sentence is written down rather than left as a gap in a spreadsheet.
- **V17 WebRTC — 12 requirements, conditional.** There is no peer-to-peer, and PRD §2.3 gates it on four
  measured conditions rather than on intent. The trigger is those conditions being met.
- **V9 Self-contained Tokens — 7 requirements, conditional.** §13.2 fixes what a relay admission token may do
  and not what shape it is. The trigger is that shape turning out to be a self-contained token.

**V6 Authentication is the largest applicability question and it is deliberately not answered here.** Its 47
requirements assume passwords, lockout, credential recovery and MFA enrollment; row 12 selected a passkey-only
credential and rows 13 and 14 rejected stretching entirely. **Many of them are inapplicable not because the
feature is absent but because the design chose a shape the requirement does not contemplate** — a distinction
that matters, because "we do not do that" and "we do something the requirement did not anticipate" are
recorded very differently. The chapter stays in scope and the per-requirement dispositions are produced at
verification, with that reason attached to each.

---

## 4. The one requirement about what this product actually is, and it fails

`V14.3.3` (L2): _data stored in browser storage (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, cookies) does not
contain sensitive data, with the exception of session tokens._

**The entire content of the application is user data in IndexedDB. That is what a local-first application is.**
So the profile's floor contains a requirement the product does not meet as written and cannot.

It is recorded as a **deviation with a compensating control** rather than quietly dispositioned away: every
record is sealed before it is written, under a content-key generation whose key material is a non-extractable
handle that is never present in a store (§6.1, §13.2, §13.3), and §11.1's no-plaintext-at-rest test inspects a
profile snapshot at genesis, at Local, at Account and after deletion, retention expiry and migration — so the
claim is exercised rather than asserted.

**And this is the single most useful line in the profile**, because of what sits beside it. Searched against
the published requirement text:

| Term the design depends on | Requirements in ASVS 5.0.0 mentioning it |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| browser storage            | **1** — V14.3.3, the one above           |
| Trusted Types              | **0**                                    |
| service worker             | **0**                                    |
| offline                    | **0**                                    |

**ASVS 5.0.0 does not model an application of this shape.** That is a fact about what the standard is for
rather than a criticism of it — it is written for applications with a server that holds and processes user
data, and here the server is content-blind by construction (§7.2) and frequently absent (§7.1). The honest
response is a recorded deviation and a named addendum, **not a level chosen high enough to look thorough.**

---

## 5. The addendum was already written, in §10.9

Five controls the standard does not carry at any level. **None of them is invented here**, which is most of the
argument for them: §10.9 wrote the list while explaining why the cryptographic boundary is a web origin, and
the addendum is the part of that list ASVS has no requirement for.

| #   | Control                                                                                                         | Method | Where it is verified                          |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| A1  | **No remote origin referenced in built output**, allowlisted namespace identifiers aside. Not "with SRI" — none | CI     | `scripts/check-origin-isolation.mjs`, **now** |
| A2  | Trusted Types enforced where the platform supports it                                                           | CI     | §11.2 test 14, at Stage 4                     |
| A3  | Service-worker update integrity                                                                                 | review | Stage 4                                       |
| A4  | Everything an app-managed store holds is ciphertext, from genesis, every device                                 | CI     | §11.1's no-plaintext-at-rest test             |
| A5  | No control may be weakened by being offline, or require the network to hold                                     | review | Stage 4                                       |

**A1 is stronger than the requirement it supersedes, and the difference is the point.** V3.6.1 permits external
hosting with Subresource Integrity. SRI pins a byte string; it does not remove the party. Under §10.9 a
third-party asset in this origin is inside the end-to-end boundary whether or not its hash was checked, so the
control is _none_ rather than _verified_.

**A5 is the one that will be hardest to verify and is stated anyway.** ASVS assumes a server is reachable. Here
it frequently is not, and §13.9 already turns on that distinction — a slot verifier that only worked online
would be a different product.

---

## 6. "Repeatable" is the word doing the work, so the profile is built rather than written

§13.11 asks for _repeatable verification_. A profile in prose is a document that agrees with the system on the
day it is written; the project's answer everywhere else has been to put the check in the build, and there is no
reason for this row to be the exception.

**So the profile is generated, and it checks itself on every `pnpm check`:**

- **Chapters are discovered from the pinned index, never from a list beside it.** A hand-maintained list is how
  a later version's new chapter would arrive undispositioned — the same argument that made
  `check-aad-coverage.mjs` glob for generators.
- Every exclusion carries a reason; every conditional exclusion carries a trigger.
- Every pulled-up requirement **exists, is genuinely L3, and is in a chapter that is in scope**. A pull-up of
  something already inside the floor says nothing; a pull-up out of an excluded chapter is a contradiction.
- Every deviation names a requirement that **is** inside the floor, a compensating control, and the section
  that makes it true.
- **Every addendum control cites a section that exists in the TRD**, and where it claims CI verification, the
  named check has to exist on disk.
- The counts reconcile against the index.

**The last of those bit during construction, which is the argument for having it.** A4 was written as a Stage 1
CI control with no check named — true in spirit, since §11.1 already owes the test, and a claim with no address
in fact. The rule now distinguishes a check that exists from a **planned** check, and a planned check has to
name a §11 test the TRD already owes. The generator refused the profile until it did.

**The standard is pinned, not fetched.** `pnpm check` never reaches the network: a build step that does turns a
third party's publishing schedule into a build failure. `scripts/fetch-asvs-index.mjs --check` (as
`pnpm asvs:pin`) compares against the published file deliberately, and a drift is something to read rather than
something to break the build.

**Identifiers and levels are pinned; requirement text is not.** ASVS is CC BY-SA 4.0. A derived index of
identifiers and levels is what the profile needs, reproducing the prose is not, and the attribution travels in
the file.

---

## 7. What it costs

| Cost             | Measured or bounded                                                     | Against                                                   |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bundle           | **None**                                                                | The profile is a build artifact, not shipped code         |
| Build            | One scan of `dist/` after `check-budget.mjs`, on the same 6 files       | `pnpm build`, which already reads them                    |
| Repository       | 9 kB of pinned index — identifiers and levels for 345 requirements      | Once per ASVS version                                     |
| Ongoing          | A version bump is a deliberate act: rerun the fetcher, re-read the diff | Not automatic, on purpose                                 |
| **Verification** | **218 requirements, most at Stage 4**                                   | The real cost, and it is level 2's rather than this row's |

---

## 8. What Stage 4 owes, and what is still open

**Owed, and only A1 is discharged.** The profile records methods; the verification is §13.11's gate before
Stage 4 ships (sequencing §3.7). What Stage 4 has to produce is the per-requirement worksheet for the 218,
with V6's dispositions carrying §3's distinction, plus the four remaining addendum controls.

**One thing is discharged now and should be**, because it was the one control that could be. `pnpm build`
fails if any built file references a remote origin, and the check was tested in both directions — a
`fonts.googleapis.com` stylesheet added to `dist/index.html` fails it, and removing it passes again. It is the
control §10.9 names first and the one a font link would regress silently.

**It was doing less than this sentence said, and `S0-1` fixed the check rather than the sentence**
(`f-5bd9552-origin-scan-static-forms`). The scanner failed on **seven literal fetch syntaxes** — `src`, `href`,
`url()`, `@import`, static and dynamic imports, `importScripts` — and classified every other remote URL as a
non-failing _mention_, while printing _the key-holding origin is first-party only_. So a
`fetch("https://third.example/code")`, a `WebSocket`, a URL handed to `setAttribute`, or a worker constructor
passed. **A font link was the case it was written for and the case it caught; the ones that matter more were
outside the list.**

**The default inverts, and the measurement is why that is cheap.** Every remote origin in built output is now a
violation unless allowlisted with a reason. `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` was already empty — no remote origin may be
referenced at all — so the fetching/mention distinction never had a policy behind it. Scanning the current
build finds **one** remote origin, `http://www.w3.org`, and every occurrence is an XML namespace identifier the
DOM requires by name. **One entry, and it is a category rather than a party.**

**A1's claim is now the size of its evidence.** What the check proves is that no literal remote URL appears in
built output; what it cannot see is a URL assembled from parts, or code fetched and then evaluated. That
residual belongs to CSP — `default-src 'self'`, `connect-src 'self'`, `frame-ancestors 'none'` — which is
listed below as open and which A1 now explicitly leans on rather than implying it has covered.

**Open, and offered to 3b rather than answered here.**

- **Whether the profile should be ASVS at all, given §4.** A reviewer who thinks a standard covering this
  product's storage model in one requirement is the wrong instrument should say so, and the alternative is
  probably _no external standard plus a longer addendum_ rather than a different standard. That is worth an
  opinion from someone outside the project, and it is the sort of question level 2 exists to have asked.
- **Whether V6's per-requirement dispositions can be written before Stage 4 builds the account service.** §3
  argues they carry a distinction that only makes sense against a built flow; a reviewer may reasonably think
  the distinction is clear enough now.
- **CSP's actual directive set**, which is where A1, A2 and V3.4.3 meet and is a Stage 4 artifact rather than a
  selection. **Three directives are now load-bearing rather than merely advisable** (`S0-1`):
  `default-src 'self'` and `connect-src 'self'` are what covers the runtime half A1's static scan cannot see,
  and `frame-ancestors 'none'` is what makes TRD §13.9's framed WebAuthn ceremony unreachable. The as-built
  readback of all three is a release gate, and until it exists both controls stand on their repository-side
  halves alone — which is stated here rather than assumed.
